title: The computer that burbles
teaches: LFO shapes, sample-and-hold, tempo sync and retrigger

blocks.text: **The sound.** In science-fiction films of the 1960s and 70s, a computer at work made a particular noise: a stream of bubbling, random blips, as though it were muttering to itself. Real computers made no such sound.[^real-computers] The noise came from synthesizers, and it is still the shorthand for a machine thinking. Here is a held note, and the same note burbling.

blocks.caption: A held note, and the same note thinking

blocks.text: The burble is the LFO from lesson 4, moving the filter's cutoff, as it did for the wah. What is different is the *shape* of its movement. A sine glides smoothly up and down. This one jumps to a new place at random, sixteen times a bar, and stays there until the next jump.

An LFO, like an audio oscillator, can have a shape: the path it takes from top to bottom and back. Most synths offer the same few. A **sine** or a **triangle** glides, the triangle at a steady speed. A **saw** rises steadily and drops at once, or the reverse. A **square** sits at the top, then jumps to the bottom and sits there.

On pitch, the shapes are easy to tell apart. The figure below has the LFO set to pitch, a semitone deep, twice a bar. The sine is a gentle wobble. The square flips between two notes, which is a **trill**. The saw climbs and snaps back like a siren that keeps restarting.

blocks.caption: The LFO on pitch. Step through its shapes.

blocks.text: The fifth shape, **S&H**, is the odd one out. It has no regular shape at all. It is random.

**Sample and hold** is a circuit with one job. A clock ticks; at each tick, the circuit takes the value of whatever is plugged into it, and holds that value steady until the next tick.[^circuit] Plug noise into it, and every tick picks a new random value out of the hiss. The output is a staircase: a level, then a jump to another level, then another, with no pattern.

blocks.caption: Noise, sampled at each tick of a clock and held until the next. Speed up the clock.
blocks.task: Speed the clock up to 32 ticks a bar or more

blocks.text: Slowly clocked, it makes a few big random moves. Clocked once per note, it gives each note its own random brightness, so a repeated note never sounds quite the same twice. Clocked fast, the steps are so close that the staircase almost follows the noise itself. The film computers sat in the middle: a new random value every sixteenth note, sent to a resonant filter, so that every step is heard as a vowel-like blip.

An LFO's speed can be set two ways. Free, it is a rate in hertz, cycles per second, and it drifts against whatever else is playing. **Synced**, it is counted in notes of the beat: once a bar, once a quarter note, once a sixteenth. Change the tempo and a synced LFO keeps step. This synth's LFO is always synced, which is why its rate knob reads in bars and notes.

blocks.caption: Sample and hold on a resonant filter. Speed it up and deepen it.
blocks.task: Rate at 1/8 or faster, depth at 65 % or more

blocks.text: The other choice is where each cycle starts. A **free-running** LFO carries on through every note, so each note catches it somewhere different. A **retriggered** one restarts at each new note, so every note gets the same movement: a vibrato that always starts at its middle, or a rise that begins from the bottom. This synth restarts its LFO each time the loop comes round, and lets it run free when you play the keys yourself. Many synths also offer **smooth random**: the S&H's steps with glides between them, a slow, aimless wander that suits a drifting pad.[^uncertainty]

Now the burble. Its parts: the LFO's random shape, sent to the cutoff, fast enough to be busy, deep enough to be heard, and a resonance high enough that each step rings. The resonance is set low here, the LFO is a slow sine on pitch, and the depth is at zero.

blocks.caption: A resonant saw with an idle LFO. Make the computer think.

blocks.text: Point the same random staircase at the pitch instead, and the computer starts playing random notes: another sound from the same films. Point it at the pulse width, and each step gets a slightly different hollowness. Randomness, used gently, is one of the main ways a synth player stops a sound being mechanical.

blocks.caption: Five questions on LFO shapes
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A square LFO is sent to pitch. What do you hear?
items.why: A square sits at the top, then at the bottom: two pitches, alternating.

items.ask: What does sample and hold do?
choices: Takes a value at each clock tick and holds it until the next
Records a sample of the sound
Holds the last note while the key is up
items.why: It samples whatever is plugged in, usually noise, at each tick, and holds it.

items.ask: Sample and hold on noise, clocked very fast. What does the output look like?
choices: Almost the noise itself, in tiny steps
items.why: The faster the clock, the more closely the staircase follows what it samples.

items.ask: What does 'synced' mean for an LFO's rate?
choices: It is counted in notes of the beat, and follows the tempo
It runs at a fixed number of hertz
items.why: A synced rate is a fraction of a bar, so it keeps step when the tempo changes.

items.ask: What does retriggering an LFO do?
choices: Restarts it at each new note, so every note gets the same movement
items.why: A free-running LFO is caught wherever it happens to be; a retriggered one starts afresh.

summary: **An LFO has a shape**: sine and triangle glide, saw ramps and drops, square jumps between two levels.
**A square LFO on pitch is a trill**; a saw on pitch is a siren that keeps restarting.
**Sample and hold** takes a value at each clock tick and holds it until the next.
**S&H on noise gives a random staircase**; on a resonant filter, the burbling film computer.
**A synced LFO counts in notes of the beat** and keeps step with the tempo.
**A retriggered LFO restarts at each note**; a free-running one carries on through them.
**Smooth random** glides between random values, for slow, aimless movement.

circuit.title: The circuit
circuit.text: In its simplest form, sample and hold is a switch and a capacitor. At each tick the switch closes for an instant and the capacitor charges to the input's voltage; then the switch opens and the capacitor keeps that voltage until the next tick. Every digital recording starts with the same circuit, sampling the microphone's voltage tens of thousands of times a second.

uncertainty.title: The Source of Uncertainty
uncertainty.text: Don Buchla's modular synthesizers of the late 1960s had a module called the Source of Uncertainty, a box of random voltages: noise, stepped random values, and smoothly wandering ones. Buchla wanted instruments that would surprise the player, and random modulation has been a fixture of synths ever since.

real-computers.title: What 1960s computers actually sounded like
real-computers.text: A real mainframe room was loud, but the noise was mechanical: cooling fans, spinning magnetic tape drives, card readers, and line printers hammering paper. A few early machines did have a small speaker wired to a register in the processor so engineers could hear when a programme was stuck in a loop, and bored operators soon worked out how to make them buzz out simple tunes.
